Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp.'s Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are Mike Harlan, Chief Executive Officer; John Hargrove, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Tom Rivera, VP of Exploration; Emily Patel, VP of Marketing; and David Greene, Chief Sustainability Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to Mike Harlan.

Mike Harlan: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp. delivered solid results in Q3, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved record production volumes averaging 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day, with oil up 5% quarter-over-quarter and 14% year-over-year, reflecting successful ramp-ups in the Permian and contributions from our Guyana stake. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on exploration and drilling, where we spudded 28 wells with a 97% success rate and IP30 rates up 18% sequentially, unlocking high-return inventory in the Delaware Basin and beyond. We are focused on refining segment outperformance, with throughput at 2.42 million barrels per day and margins at $18.20 per barrel. Further, we are working on midstream expansion, hitting record transportation volumes of 3.2 million BOE per day. We continue to adjust to operating expenses per BOE at $9.85, down 7% sequentially through digital initiatives and water management. We are advancing hedging programs that added $210 million to EBITDA. Finally, we are taking steps to develop our resource potential, with plans for 650,000 to 700,000 BOE per day by 2028 backed by 15 billion BOE unrisked resources.

Now, I'll turn the call over to John Hargrove to discuss our financial results in more detail.

John Hargrove: Thank you, Mike. As Mike mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.8 billion, up 15% year-over-year. Operating income was $650 million, and net income was $420 million. We generated $750 million in free cash flow and returned $300 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $4.2 billion in debt and $1.8 billion in cash.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining our Q3 earnings call. I'll now dive into our realized pricing performance, with a particular focus on the impact of our hedging programs, which continue to be a cornerstone of our risk management strategy here at Apex Energy. We operate a diversified portfolio primarily in the Permian Basin for oil and the Haynesville Shale for natural gas, with some exposure in the Eagle Ford. Our hedging discipline has been critical amid the volatility we've seen this quarter, driven by persistent OPEC+ production cuts, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and softer demand signals from China.

Let me start with crude oil realized prices. In Q3, our realized oil price averaged $76.45 per barrel, down about 8% sequentially from $83.20 in Q2 but still up 12% year-over-year. For context, the NYMEX WTI benchmark averaged $81.50 per barrel during the quarter, while Brent held steady around $85.20. Our realized price reflects a few key dynamics: first, our Permian WTI differential averaged a tight -$2.75 per barrel, benefiting from improved midstream infrastructure like the Matterhorn Express Pipeline coming online, which alleviated some Waha hub bottlenecks we saw last year. Second, location and quality adjustments shaved off another -$1.30 per barrel net, as our light sweet crude commanded a modest premium over WTI in Gulf Coast markets.

Now, turning to the impact of our hedging programs – this is where we protected significant value. We had approximately 65% of our Q3 oil production hedged through a mix of swaps and collars. Specifically, swaps covered 40% of volumes at a fixed floor of $72.00 per barrel. Collars on the remaining 25% had an average floor of $70.50 and ceiling of $88.00 per barrel. Without these hedges, our realized oil price would have been $74.10 per barrel – a $2.35 per barrel drag from lower spot prices in late quarter when WTI dipped below $80 on inventory builds reported by the EIA. The hedges added $152 million to our oil revenues quarter-over-quarter, equivalent to about 15% of our total upstream EBITDA. This layered approach – where we stagger maturities across 12-36 months – allowed us to capture upside in early Q3 when WTI spiked to $87 on supply disruption fears from the Red Sea, while providing a floor during the pullback.

Looking forward, we remain opportunistically hedged: 55% of Q4 oil volumes are protected with floors averaging $73.50, and 45% for Q1 next year at $74.20. For 2025 full-year, we've locked in 50% of projected production at $72.80, and we're eyeing additional collars if the forward curve – currently backwardated to $78 for Q1 – inverts further.

Shifting to natural gas realized prices, which were a bright spot despite broader market weakness. Our Q3 realized gas price came in at $3.15 per MCF, a robust 18% increase from $2.67 in Q2 and up 25% year-over-year. Henry Hub spot averaged $3.45 per MCF, pressured by a warmer-than-normal shoulder season and elevated storage levels at 2.3 Bcf/d above the five-year average per EIA data. Our Haynesville basis differential improved to -$0.25 per MCF from -$0.45 in Q2, thanks to stronger LNG export demand via the Golden Pass facility ramp-up and better connectivity to the Texas Eastern Transmission system.

Hedging played an even bigger role here, with 75% of Q3 gas production covered: basis swaps hedged 30% against Henry Hub plus Haynesville differentials, locking in $3.00 per MCF net. NYMEX swaps on 45% at an average $2.95 per MCF. This program shielded us from a $0.40 per MCF spot market decline in late quarter, when Henry Hub traded as low as $2.60 amid production surges from Appalachia. Absent hedges, realized prices would have been $2.72 per MCF, costing us $48 million in forgone revenue – or roughly 8% of segment EBITDA. Our strategy emphasizes basis protection given Haynesville's regional dynamics, and we've layered in fixed-price swaps to capitalize on the contango in the 2025 strip, currently at $3.80 for winter months.

In aggregate, our hedging programs contributed $210 million to Q3 adjusted EBITDA – about 22% of the total – while allowing us to retain 35% of volumes unhedged to capture upside. This disciplined approach aligns with peers like EOG Resources and Pioneer Natural Resources, who've similarly emphasized collars to balance free cash flow generation with shareholder returns. Strategically, we're enhancing our program with algorithmic trading overlays tied to EIA weekly storage reports and CME futures curves, aiming to boost hedge effectiveness to 80%+ in coming quarters. We're also exploring structured products like three-way collars to widen participation ranges without capping too much upside.

Regionally, Permian's resilience underscores our focus on low-cost inventory – our D&C breakevens remain at $45 WTI equivalent – while Haynesville positions us for LNG-driven demand growth, with Freeport LNG at full capacity by year-end. We see realized prices stabilizing as winter heating demand kicks in and OPEC+ quotas hold, but volatility remains, hence our proactive hedging stance.

Turning now to our Refining segment, which remains a cornerstone of our integrated model, delivering robust results in the quarter despite some volatility in global crude differentials and product cracks. I'll walk you through the key metrics—throughput, margins, and operational efficiency—with a focus on what drove our outperformance and our strategic positioning moving forward.

Starting with throughput: We achieved average net throughput of 2.42 million barrels per day across our six high-complexity refineries, representing 94% utilization of our 2.58 million barrels per day nameplate capacity. This marks a 7% increase quarter-over-quarter from Q2's 2.26 million bpd and a solid 4% year-over-year gain. The uptick was primarily driven by strong domestic demand recovery in PADD 3—the U.S. Gulf Coast—where gasoline consumption rebounded 12% YoY amid summer driving season and pent-up mobility, coupled with elevated diesel exports to Europe amid ongoing supply constraints from the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Regionally, our flagship Port Arthur complex in Texas ran at 98% utilization, processing a diverse slate including 650,000 bpd of light sweet WTI Midland and imported Saharan crudes, benefiting from favorable LLS-WTI spreads averaging $4.50 per barrel. In the Midwest, our Joliet and Lima facilities averaged 92% utilization, supported by Canadian heavy sour imports via the Keystone Pipeline, while our West Coast Mandan refinery operated at 88% amid softer regional demand but offset by robust Jet A exports to Asia. Notably, we minimized unplanned downtime to just 0.5% through proactive predictive maintenance using our AI-driven asset management platform, which flagged potential issues in our FCC units two weeks ahead of schedule.

Moving to margins: Our realized refining margin came in at an impressive $18.20 per barrel, well above our long-term average of $14 and up 15% from Q2's $15.80. This was fueled by strong crack spreads across the slate: our USGC 3-2-1 crack averaged $22.50 per barrel, 20% richer than the NYMEX benchmark, while diesel cracks held firm at $28 per barrel on the back of global trucking and marine bunker demand post-IMO 2020 sulfur regs. Gasoline RBOB cracks were $18, benefiting from ethanol blending mandates and seasonal Reid Vapor Pressure compliance.

Product optimization played a big role here—we shifted yields toward high-margin ULSD and renewable diesel precursors, achieving a 52/30/18 distillate/gasoline/residual split versus our typical 48/32/20. Our proprietary alkylation expansion at Port Arthur boosted octane giveaway by 1.2 RON, adding $1.10 per barrel to gasoline margins, while hydrocracker throughput rose 10% QoQ to capitalize on the diesel premium. Feedstock costs were well-controlled at $68 per barrel blended, thanks to opportunistic LCO imports from India at a $6 discount to Brent. Comparatively, this outpaced peers like Phillips 66 and Marathon Petroleum, whose Gulf Coast margins trailed by $2-3 per barrel due to heavier turnaround schedules.

On operational efficiency, we continue to lead the industry with cash operating costs of $4.60 per barrel, down 8% YoY and 3% from Q2, reflecting our relentless focus on digital transformation and complexity leverage—our portfolio Nelson Complexity Index averages 11.2, enabling superior middle distillate yields of 54%. Key initiatives included the completion of our semi-annual turnaround at Corpus Christi, where we installed new high-severity hydrotreaters compliant with Tier 3 emissions standards ahead of 2025 EPA deadlines, at a cost of just $120 million versus budgeted $140 million. Energy intensity improved 5% to 85,000 BTU per barrel through cogeneration optimizations and flare minimization, reducing Scope 1 emissions by 12% QoQ.

We also advanced our sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) transition, commissioning a 10,000 bpd renewable diesel unit at Mandan using HEFA technology on waste soybean oil feedstocks, capturing $45 per barrel cracks amid Biden administration blender tax credits. This positions us to hit 20% biofuels in our product slate by 2026, ahead of EU mandates and ahead of competitors like Chevron.

Strategically, we're prudently positioned for next year with $1.2 billion in planned maintenance capex, targeting 92-95% utilization. We'll continue optimizing crude slates via our 1.5 million bpd of advantaged logistics—pipelines like EPIC and terminals on the USGC—to arbitrage WTI-Brent contango, expected at $5-7 per barrel. Risks include potential Canadian rail disruptions impacting sour heavy supply, but our inventory buffers and spot market flexibility mitigate this. Overall, Refining contributed $850 million in segment EBITDA, up 22% YoY, underscoring our resilience in a $75-85 WTI environment.

I'll now dive into our operating expenses per BOE, where we've continued to demonstrate industry-leading cost discipline amid a volatile macro environment. As you know, operating expenses per BOE—or what we primarily track as lease operating expenses, or LOE, plus associated workover and maintenance costs—remain a critical metric for assessing operational efficiency in our upstream portfolio. This quarter, we delivered LOE of $9.85 per BOE, a 7% sequential improvement from $10.60 in Q2 and a robust 18% year-over-year decline from $12.00 last year. 

First, on the trend analysis: Over the past five quarters, we've engineered a steady downward trajectory in OPEX per BOE, from a cyclical peak of $13.20 in Q1 last year—driven by post-pandemic supply chain disruptions and elevated workover activity—to our current $9.85 run-rate. This represents a cumulative 25% reduction, outpacing peers like Pioneer Natural Resources, which reported around $8-9 per BOE in the Permian but with a flatter trajectory, and significantly better than Occidental's blended $11-12 across their assets. Breaking it down regionally:

Permian Basin (65% of production): Our flagship asset here clocked in at $7.20 per BOE this quarter, down 22% YoY. This reflects the basin's structural advantages—proximity to midstream infrastructure and economies of scale from our 1,200+ well pads. Sequential gains came from reduced salt water disposal costs, which fell 15% to $1.10 per BOE via optimized recycling rates now exceeding 85%, up from 70% last year.

Eagle Ford Shale (25% of production): LOE here improved to $10.50 per BOE, a 12% YoY drop, despite gas-heavy production facing Henry Hub pricing pressure at $2.50/MMBtu. Key was dialing back artificial lift expenses on our gas wells by 20% through variable speed drive upgrades on ESPs.

Gulf of Mexico Shelf (10% of production): This higher-cost bucket came in at $18.40 per BOE, flat QoQ but 10% below prior year, cushioned by deferred subsea interventions. Offshore remains our margin tail, but it's accretive given realizations 20% above WTI.

Overall, this $2.15 per BOE YoY savings equated to $180 million in annual run-rate cash flow preservation at our average production. 

Now, turning to our cost management strategies—these aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our "Efficiency 2.0" playbook, targeting sub-$9 per BOE blended by year-end 2025. Here's how we're executing:

1. Digital and Automation Initiatives (30% of savings): We've rolled out AI-driven predictive maintenance across 80% of our Permian fleet, leveraging tools like Halliburton's DecisionSpace 365 platform. This has cut unplanned downtime by 25%, slashing workover costs from $1.80 to $1.40 per BOE. In the Eagle Ford, our digital twin models for hydraulic fracturing optimization reduced proppant and chemical intensity by 10-15%, directly flowing to LOE.

2. Supply Chain and Vendor Optimization (25% of savings): Post-UAE supply disruptions earlier this year, we locked in 18-month take-or-pay contracts for tubular goods and frac sand at 15% below 2023 peaks, saving $0.50 per BOE. We're also consolidating service providers—now down to top-tier partners like SLB and Baker Hughes for 70% of work—to extract volume-based rebates averaging 8-10%.

3. Water and Emissions Management (20% of savings): In the water-scarce Permian, our produced water pipeline network, now spanning 500 miles and integrated with WaterBridge partnerships, has boosted recycling to 88%, trimming disposal costs by $0.80 per BOE. Electrification efforts—converting 40% of field power to grid and renewables—have halved diesel fuel expenses, aligning with our net-zero by 2040 commitments and dodging potential carbon taxes.

4. Regional Tailoring and Portfolio Rationalization (15% of savings): We're high-grading: Divesting non-core Eagle Ford legacy wells with >$15/BOE LOE, while accelerating Permian D&C on Tier 1 acreage yielding sub-$6/BOE full-cycle costs. Offshore, we're partnering with supermajors like Chevron on shared subsea infrastructure to amortize fixed costs.

5. Hedging and Inflation Hedges (10% of savings): With WTI averaging $75/bbl this quarter, our layered swaps cover 60% of 2025 oil at $72, insulating against input inflation. We've also indexed 30% of service contracts to CPI minus productivity gains.

Looking forward, we see OPEX per BOE stabilizing at $9.50-$10.00 in Q1 next year, assuming Brent at $75-80 and no major weather events, before resuming decline to $8.80 by year-end. Risks include rig count inflation pressuring labor rates—up 5% industry-wide—or prolonged low gas prices necessitating more curtailments. But our strategies position us in the first quartile versus E&P peers, with ROCE expanding 300 bps to 18% on the back of these efficiencies.

I will now turn the call over to Lisa Chen for an operational update.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, John. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought new Delaware Basin wells online, which are expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives.

Thank you, Mike. Let's dive into our production volumes for the third quarter, which continue to demonstrate the strength of our operational execution amid a supportive commodity price environment. WTI crude averaged around $82 per barrel during the quarter, while Henry Hub natural gas held steady near $2.80 per MMBtu, providing solid realizations across our portfolio.

Starting with the headline numbers: our total net production averaged 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in Q3, marking a robust 3.6% increase quarter-over-quarter from 275,000 BOE/d in Q2, and an impressive 9.6% year-over-year lift from 260,000 BOE/d in Q3 2023. This outperformance reflects the successful ramp-up of our 2024 drilling program, particularly in the Permian Basin, where we've leaned into our multi-bench development strategy.

Breaking it down by commodity:

Oil production hit a record 210,000 barrels per day, up 5% QoQ from 200,000 bbl/d in Q2 and 14% YoY from 184,000 bbl/d last year. The QoQ growth was driven by initial production rates from 28 new Delaware Basin wells brought online in the Northwest Shelf, where average 30-day IPs exceeded 1,800 bbl/d of oil per well—our strongest quarter yet. These wells benefited from our enhanced completions design: 5,000-foot laterals with 2,500 pounds of proppant per foot and diverter technology, which improved stage-level efficiency by 15% compared to Q2. YoY, oil volumes surged thanks to the full-year contribution from our Q4 2023 acquisition of the 15,000 net acre Bravo prospect in the Midland Basin, adding about 12,000 bbl/d of high-quality, 42-degree API sweet crude.

Natural gas production, net to us after processing and third-party volumes, averaged 930,000 Mcf/d, equivalent to 75,000 BOE/d after our standard 6:1 Mcf-to-BOE conversion. This was flat QoQ from Q2's 930,000 Mcf/d but up 5% YoY from 885,000 Mcf/d in Q3 2023. The stability QoQ reflects seasonal shut-ins in the Eagle Ford for maintenance on our Agua Dulce plant, which processes about 40% of our South Texas gas, offset by richer gas cuts from new Permian completions—our associated gas now yields 85 BTU with strong NGL content at 120 bbl/MMcf. YoY gains came from debottlenecking our Pecos County gas plant to 150 MMcf/d capacity, reducing curtailments that plagued us last year during the winter storm analogs.

Regionally, the Permian Basin—our core growth engine, comprising 72% of total volumes—delivered 205,000 BOE/d, up 5.5% QoQ and 12% YoY, fueled by 12 operated pads turned-to-flow and non-op activity on our 40% working interest in the Waha Hub area. We're seeing base declines of just 8% annualized there, below the basin average of 12%, thanks to our child-parent well sequencing and refracturing pilots, which recovered an additional 10% EUR per section.

In the Eagle Ford, volumes held at 45,000 BOE/d, down slightly 2% QoQ due to deferred completions amid low gas prices but up 4% YoY from optimized drilling inventory. Our Black Oil window continues to shine, with oil cuts over 65%, and we're testing nano-proppant additives to boost propped fracture conductivity by 20%.

Internationally, our 5% stake in the ExxonMobil-led Stabroek Block offshore Guyana contributed a steady 15,000 BOE/d of high-margin oil, unchanged QoQ and up 20% YoY post the Payara Phase 1 startup. FPSO Liza Destiny is firing on all cylinders at 220,000 bbl/d gross, and we're excited about Yellowtail FID later this year.

Strategically, these results underscore our shift toward oil-weighted growth—oil now 74% of total BOE, up from 71% YoY—while managing gas through aggressive hedging: 75% of Q4 gas volumes hedged at $3.25/MMBtu strip. We've reduced our Permian D&C breakevens to $42/bbl WTI equivalent through supply chain optimizations with Halliburton and Liberty Oilfield Services, positioning us for 10-15% annual production growth into 2025.

Looking ahead, we guide Q4 total production to 290,000-300,000 BOE/d, with oil at 215,000-220,000 bbl/d, assuming no major weather disruptions or midstream constraints. This sets us up well against peers like Pioneer and Occidental in the Permian consolidation wave.

Now I will turn it over to Tom Rivera for an update on our exploration activities.

Tom Rivera: Thank you, Lisa. We are excited about the potential of our exploration program. We recently completed a successful seismic survey in the Delaware Basin and are planning to drill 115 to 125 exploration wells in the next year. We believe these wells have the potential to add significant reserves to our portfolio.

Thanks, and good morning, everyone. I'm excited to dive into our exploration and drilling updates today. As you know, our E&D program remains the cornerstone of our growth strategy, driving high-margin inventory additions and robust returns in this $75 to $85 WTI environment. We've maintained capital discipline while pushing the envelope on technical innovation, and the results are speaking for themselves. Let me walk you through the key well results from Q3, regional highlights, and our forward plans.

Starting with the headline numbers: In Q3, we spudded 28 wells across our core acreage, brought online 32 wells, and achieved a drilling success rate of 97%—our best quarter on record. Average initial production, or IP30, came in at 1,450 boe per day per well, up 18% sequentially and 32% year-over-year, thanks to optimized completions and landing zones. Our drilled but uncompleted, or DUC, inventory stands at 45 wells, giving us strong line-of-sight production growth into 2025. Estimated ultimate recovery, or EUR, on these new wells averages 1.2 MMboe, with drilling and completion costs down to $7.2 million per well—a 22% reduction from last year, driven by supply chain efficiencies and our in-house PDC bit program.

Let's break it down by region, starting with the Permian Basin, which accounted for 65% of our activity. In the Delaware Basin, our Northern Howard County asset—recently bolstered by the $1.2 billion acquisition from a private seller akin to our 2023 SM Energy deal—delivered standout results. The "Howard 12H-14H" three-well pad targeted the Wolfcamp A and B benches with 14,500-foot laterals and our proprietary 65-stage slickwater frac design, incorporating 2,200 pounds of proppant per foot. These wells flowed at an IP30 of 2,100 boe/d (82% oil), shattering our type curve by 25% and posting an NPV-10 of $14 million at current strips. We've identified 450 drilling locations here with EURs north of 1.5 MMboe, and seismic reprocessing using full-waveform inversion has unlocked an additional 120 locations in the Second Bone Spring.

Moving south to the Midland Basin, our Glasscock County program emphasized stack pay development. The "Midland Stack 5-well pad" in the Upper Spraberry through Wolfcamp D tested simultaneous frac operations, or SIMOPS, reducing cycle times to 45 days from spud to sales—10 days faster than peers like Pioneer. IP30 averaged 1,100 boe/d with 78% oil, and we're seeing 15% better half-cycle returns due to our recycled produced water usage, now at 92% on all pads, aligning with our net-zero methane goals ahead of 2026.

In the Eagle Ford, which makes up 25% of our E&D capex, we hit paydirt with our first Karnes County hybrid completions. The "Karnes Deep 3H" well, drilled to 3,200 feet TVD with a 10,000-foot lateral targeting the Lower Eagle Ford shale, posted an IP30 of 1,800 boe/d (75% liquids), with EURs modeled at 950 Mboe. This outperforms our legacy vertical wells by 40%, validating our shift to horizontals. We've derisked 180 locations here, and with natural gas prices holding at $2.80 Henry Hub, these wells deliver IRRs over 60% at $70 WTI equivalent.

Offshore, our Gulf of Mexico shallow-water program yielded mixed but promising results. The "Eagle Pass #3" appraisal well in Eugene Island Block 308 confirmed 15 MMboe of 2P reserves at 35 API gravity, with a stabilized rate of 4,200 boe/d. While we encountered some mechanical issues delaying tie-in, we've sanctioned development with a subsea tieback to our existing West Delta infrastructure, targeting first oil in Q2 2025 at under $25 boe D&C costs—competitive with Chevron's Anchor project economics.

On the international front, our 15% working interest in the Exxon-led Stabroek Block offshore Guyana continues to shine. The "Yellowtail-2" appraisal well, which we participated in during Q3, exceeded pre-drill estimates with 300 feet of high-quality Liza pay, adding 200 MMboe to the block's 11 billion barrel resource base. Payout remains swift, with our share generating $150 million in free cash flow this year alone.

Technically, we're leaning into data-driven innovations. Our partnership with Halliburton on the DeciFrac AI platform has improved frac stage efficiency by 12%, predicting cluster efficiency in real-time and reducing screenouts by 40%. We've also deployed SLB's NeuroFlow fiber optics across 20 Permian wells, enabling real-time inflow profiling that boosted EURs by 8% through targeted diverter stages. ESG-wise, our electric frac fleets cut emissions 35% versus diesel, and we're piloting carbon capture on two pads with Occidental's Direct Air Capture tech.

Looking ahead to Q4 and 2025, we're guiding for 115 to 125 spuds, with $1.8 billion allocated to E&D—55% Permian, 25% Eagle Ford, 15% Gulf, and 5% international. We'll run six rigs steady-state in the Permian, adding a seventh in Q1 for Delaware inventory growth. In 2025, we plan to drill 450 to 500 wells, targeting 15% production growth to 320,000 boe/d while holding capex flat at $2.9 billion, yielding 55% free cash flow margins at $80 WTI. Key catalysts include the $800 million bolt-on in the Midland's Martin County, mirroring Continental's recent deals, and farm-down talks for non-core Eagle Ford to fund offshore.

Strategically, we're focused on Tier 1 returns: every dollar drilled generates 3x recycled value through inventory adds. With 5,500 locations at 50%+ IRR, we're insulated from downturns and positioned for M&A in a consolidating basin—think our response to Diamondback-Endeavor if opportunities arise. Risks? Service inflation remains tame at 3% QoQ, but we'll monitor rig rates closely. Overall, this program's delivering the goods: high returns, low costs, and decades of inventory.

Finally, I'll turn it over to Emily Patel to discuss our marketing strategy.

Emily Patel: Thank you, Tom. We are focused on optimizing our marketing strategy to maximize the value of our production. We are seeing strong demand for refined products in the USGC market area, and we are working to expand our customer base and strengthen our relationships with existing customers. The impact of our midstream infrastructure is significant.

Operator, thank you. Now, turning to our midstream segment, which continues to deliver resilient, fee-based cash flows and positions us at the heart of North American energy infrastructure. In Q3, midstream generated $450 million in adjusted EBITDA, up 18% year-over-year and 5% sequentially, driven by record transportation volumes and the ramp-up of several key infrastructure projects. This performance underscores our strategy of leveraging high-utilization assets amid sustained upstream production growth and growing export demand.

Let's start with transportation volumes, where we saw broad-based strength across our portfolio. Total throughput volumes reached 3.2 million barrels of oil equivalent per day, or MMBoe/d, a 12% increase from last year and 4% above Q2. Breaking it down by commodity:

Crude oil volumes hit an all-time high of 2.1 MMbbl/d, up 15% YoY, primarily fueled by Permian Basin outperformance. Our EPIC Y-Grade and Crude systems in the Delaware Basin averaged 1.4 MMbbl/d utilization—operating at 95% of nameplate capacity—benefiting from WTI-Waha basis trades tightening to just $0.50/bbl thanks to incremental takeaway like the Matterhorn Express Pipeline coming online earlier this year. In the Bakken, our Dakota Access System volumes grew 8% to 450 Mbbl/d, supported by steady Three Forks production despite some winter weather disruptions.

Natural gas and NGLs were equally robust, with gas transportation at 4.8 Bcf/d, up 10% YoY on our Rockies Express and Tetco M-3 systems, driven by Appalachia dry gas exports via Cove Point LNG. NGL fractionation volumes at our Mont Belvieu facility averaged 850 Mbbl/d, a 9% YoY increase, capturing healthy ethane rejection economics with Mont Belvieu Olefins purity prices holding above $0.35/gal amid petrochemical demand from the Gulf Coast.

Regionally, the Permian remains our crown jewel, contributing 55% of midstream volumes with barrel-mile metrics up 20% to 1.2 billion barrel-miles, reflecting longer-haul deliveries to Corpus Christi refineries and export terminals like Flint Hills' Ingleside facility. Eagle Ford NGLs grew 7%, while our Eagle Ford Mainline Pipeline to Nederland saw 92% utilization. In Appalachia, Marcellus Utica gas volumes rose 12% amid LNG cargo loadings at Elba Island, though we navigated some FTC-related contract renewals successfully, locking in 85% of capacity under take-or-pay structures at $0.45/Dth.

Shifting to infrastructure development, we've invested $320 million in capex this quarter, on track for our full-year guidance of $1.2 billion. Key milestones include:

The completion of our 42-mile Permian Connector lateral, a $250 million greenfield project tying Waddell Ranch production directly into our EPIC system. This adds 200 Mbbl/d of firm capacity and is already 100% contracted through 2028 with anchor shippers like Occidental and EOG, delivering an expected IRR north of 15%.

Phase 1 of the Apex LNG Express expansion, adding 300 MMcf/d compression on our Utica laterals to support Venture Global's Plaquemines LNG ramp-up. We've also sanctioned $150 million for Phase 2, targeting FID in Q4.

Maintenance and integrity programs: We completed hydrostatic testing on 150 miles of our legacy Keystone-adjacent crude lines, enhancing reliability and complying with PHMSA's mega-rule enhancements. Digital twin initiatives using AI-driven predictive analytics from Bentley Systems have reduced unplanned downtime by 25%, optimizing compressor station efficiency across our 5,000-mile gas network.

Strategically, we're prioritizing dropdowns from our upstream joint ventures and bolt-on acquisitions to grow our 25,000 miles of pipelines and 200 MMbbl of storage. Recent market dynamics—like Brent's $85/bbl stability and Henry Hub at $3.20/MMBtu—have bolstered shipper creditworthiness, with our tariff escalators averaging 3.5% annually tied to PPI. We're mitigating commodity exposure through 92% fee-based revenues, with only 8% variable tariffs linked to volumes.

Challenges persist, including FERC policy uncertainty around GHG emissions in certificate reviews and competition from rail alternatives in Canada, where we've hedged WCS differentials via our Hardisty storage. Looking ahead, we expect Q4 volumes to grow another 3-5% sequentially, with midstream EBITDA guidance narrowed to $1.8-1.9 billion for the year, implying 16% growth.
